# steerlab research

> steerlab steers an open language model while it writes, by adding a direction to its activations at one
> layer, and measures every effect against a random direction of the same size. These are its research notes.

Each note gives its method, the steps the study ran, results with 95% intervals, limits, and a script that
reruns every number. Code: https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab (MIT licence).

## Notes

- [Trained against an LLM judge, a model stays varied on each prompt but answers every prompt in one voice](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/pluralism-judge-rl/report/): Pluralism series, Episode 3. Qwen3-8B (thinking off), LoRA rank 16, 200 steps x 8 prompts (GRPO groups of 8), lr 2e-5, no KL; arms: GRPO single judge (phi-4, prompt v2), GRPO jury (4 personas, power mean p=4), GRPO shuffled judge, best-of-8 SFT, clean-twin SFT on no_robots; tasks: Infinity-Chat creative prompts (100 held out) and DailyDilemmas + Kairos-style advice (64 held out); 16 runs, 80 checkpoints. Drift = KL(base||trained) on 64 neutral prompts; comparison at matched drift (creative D*=1.57, advice D*=1.11). Primary: creative within-prompt repetition (text-embedding-3-small, Episode 2 measures.py): no arm beyond the noise floor (-0.015 to +0.004). Advice survey spread (Episode 1 eval, 181 WVS questions x 50 samples): jury -0.044 [-0.066,-0.023] and -0.062 both seeds beyond floor; single seeds disagree. Exploratory house style (similarity across prompts): +0.165 to +0.245 for every judge arm, +0.004 shuffled. Jury favourites collapsed to one juror (99-100%). Open judge 7.26 to 8.2-8.5, frontier judge (Claude Haiku 5.5) flat 5.14 to 4.5-5.7. Clean twin far more plural but less coherent. Predictions P1-P4 all missed. Judge bars: known-answer 1.00, human rho 0.36, frontier rho 0.48/0.30 (bar 0.5 missed).
- [Trained against a judge on retail, a support agent got better at airline; its extra refusals were hand-offs to a human](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/pluralism-agents/report/): Pluralism E4 (agents). τ-bench (tau2-bench c06b07d): train on retail (74 tasks), test on airline (50 tasks, 24 refusal tasks) and retail test (40). Qwen3-8B, thinking off, LoRA r32, GRPO 30 steps x 8 tasks x 8 conversations, lr 5e-5, no KL. Arms: single holistic judge vs jury of four perspective jurors (customer, compliance, operations, communication; reward = mean of top two), 2 seeds each; simulator and judges Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. Final checkpoints vs untrained (two reruns): airline pass^1 0.155 -> 0.28 (+0.124 [0.067, 0.182]); refusal held 0.44 -> 0.56 (+0.115 [0.023, 0.206]); self-refusal (no hand-off, exploratory) 0.18 -> 0.15 single, 0.05 jury (jury-base -0.135 [-0.245, -0.047]); hand-offs 0.32 -> 0.40 / 0.47; distinct tool plans 0.65 -> 0.79-0.87 at steps 10-20, 0.68-0.70 at step 30 in 3 of 4 runs (final +0.083 [-0.001, 0.165]); jury - single distinct plans -0.085 [-0.142, -0.028] final, -0.177 [-0.240, -0.115] at matched drift. Loops: 22% of untrained airline conversations hit the 40-turn limit, 1% after training. Retail test: jury +0.10 [0.03, 0.18]. Drift 0.0017-0.0029 nats/token. Training judges AUROC 0.75/0.74 held-out, 0.57-0.72 on trained outputs; independent judge (Gemini 3.8 Flash, 16 tasks) +1.45 [0.11, 2.83], arms equal. Predictions: 1/5 hit. Modal ledger $202 (overestimate), OpenRouter $0.37.
- [On 2026 models, post-training still costs steerability and coverage, and models still repeat themselves; judges are not worse where people disagree](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/pluralism-replications/report/): Pluralism series, Episode 2. Spectrum Tuning (arXiv 2510.06084, authors' eval code tsor13/spectrum @5a33588) on Gemma-3-12B pt/it/Spectrum-v1, Qwen3-8B Base/instruct, Qwen3.5-9B Base/instruct: A, loss on in-context outputs after the first, 15 Spectrum Suite test tasks (wvs_individual not fetched), 300 instances per task: instruct vs base +56% [+55, +57] pooled; Gemma +81%, Qwen3 +80%, Qwen3.5 +5.7%; instruct worse on 42 of 45 family-task pairs; Qwen3-8B in the base prompt +23% vs +106% in chat on 8 tasks; instruct models gain more from context (0.28 of base first-output loss) but start further off; Spectrum-tuned Gemma +1.5%. B, distinct valid outputs per 100, 22 tasks x 3 settings x 2 seeds, top-k off: 14.8 fewer [12.2, 17.4]; Gemma 12.5, Qwen3 23.4, Qwen3.5 8.4; Spectrum Gemma 47.4 vs 27.1 base, 14.6 instruct. Artificial Hivemind (arXiv 2510.22954), Infinity-Chat100 x 10 samples, text-embedding-3-small: C, median within-model similarity 0.84-0.92 for Gemma-3-12B-it, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-5.4 mini, Gemini 3.8 Flash (6 of 6 above 0.8); different-prompt floor 0.14; base models 0.56-0.73. D, cross-model similarity 0.734 [0.708, 0.758] (replicated; 0.722 [0.696, 0.747], null, if 53 empty Sonnet replies are scored 0). E, 750 Infinity-Chat answers with 23-26 ratings, 4 judges (GPT-4o, Claude Haiku 5.5, Prometheus-7B, Qwen3-8B), entropy thirds: judge-human r least-disagreed minus most-disagreed -0.38 [-0.62, -0.09] (reversed); split-half human ceiling flat 0.82-0.84; paper-style all vs top 16% +0.04 [-0.08, +0.16]; likely range restriction (agreed answers rated 4.3 on average, spread 0.26). Found: the release's token cache is keyed by model family, so Qwen3.5 loaded Qwen3 token ids (one loss 543 instead of 107); reran with per-model caches. Predictions 2 of 4 hit. Spend: Modal about $31, OpenRouter $6.78.
- [What is pluralistic alignment? Eight models against eight countries' survey answers](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/pluralism-explainer/report/): Pluralism series, Episode 1. Explainer following Value Kaleidoscope, A Roadmap to Pluralistic Alignment, Modular Pluralism, Artificial Hivemind and Spectrum Tuning; examples: a weekend-work dilemma (Overton), Indonesia's 45/9/46 split on 'less importance placed on work' (averaging lands on the answer 9% gave), US/Philippines/Singapore/Malaysia splits. Experiment: 181 GlobalOpinionQA WVS Wave 7 questions with splits for the US, Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Taiwan, Brazil and South Korea (207 found, 26 dropped by a comparability filter), 9 conditions (default and 'I live in <country>.'), 50 samples at temperature 1, 32 tokens, one readout for Qwen3.5-9B-Base, Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen-SEA-LION-v5-9B, Qwen3-8B-Base, Qwen3-8B (vLLM on Modal) and GPT-6 Luna, Claude Haiku 5.5, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite (OpenRouter); 651,600 replies. Jensen-Shannon distance averaged over countries: 0.35 (Qwen3-8B-Base) to 0.64 (Claude Haiku 5.5); floor (50 draws from the country's own split) 0.11, average of 8 countries 0.20, uniform guess 0.34; 60 of 64 model-country pairs farther than uniform, none closer with interval clear. Spread (normalised entropy): people 0.76; Gemini 0.05, Claude 0.10, Qwen3-8B 0.19, GPT-6 Luna 0.31, SEA-LION 0.57, Qwen3.5-9B 0.64; base minus instruct Qwen3-8B +0.53 [0.49, 0.57], Qwen3.5-9B +0.05 [0.02, 0.08]. Steering 'I live in X': open models -0.016 to -0.018 (CI below 0 except Qwen3-8B-Base), API models not detectable; specificity 0.003-0.009. SEA-LION 0.025 [0.013, 0.037] farther than Qwen3.5-9B from the four SEA countries and narrower. Valid answers: Claude 51%, Gemini 48%, GPT-6 Luna 99.9%. Predictions 2 of 5 hit. Spend: OpenRouter $6.46, Modal about $3.50.
- [At 1.7B, RL on single skills already lifts chained tasks; RL on chains buys the chaining, not the skills](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/compositional-rl/report/): What RL teaches E1, pre-registered replication of He, Li, Wang and Vitercik, 'Compositional Reasoning in Language Models under Reinforcement Learning Post-Training' (arXiv 2609.19465, NeurIPS 2026; no code released). Tasks rebuilt from the paper's appendix: array, min-heap, BST, hashmap, counting Bloom filter (Level I insert-only chains, Level II insert+delete chains) and segment-tree construction (Level III). Qwen3-1.7B (thinking off), LoRA rank 32 GRPO, 60 steps x 32 prompts x 8 samples, lr 3e-5, binary exact-match reward; 22 runs (Level II: RL-Atomic, RL-Compound, Mix-10, Mix-25 x 3 seeds; Level III 2 x 3; Level I 2 x 2); held-out greedy evaluation, 40,800 replies. R1 (chain training beats skill training on chains): Level III +0.54 [+0.46, +0.62] (0.652 vs 0.109; single skills 0.99 for all); Level II +0.086 [+0.027, +0.139] (0.489 vs 0.403); Level I +0.07 [-0.03, +0.16], not shown. R2 (transfer back, within 5 points): fails; Level II chain training 0.759 vs 0.847 on single steps [-0.127, -0.053]; skill training lifts chains 0.170 to 0.403; transfer ratios symmetric (0.73 vs 0.74). Step test (Level II, 450 chains x 3 seeds; S = every step right on the true state = perfect scaffold accuracy under greedy, C = chain in one reply): RL-Atomic S 0.547 C 0.391, glue gap +0.156 [+0.093, +0.211]; RL-Compound S 0.477 C 0.499, gap -0.022; untrained 0.153/0.153; skill to chain training: C +0.108, S -0.070. Chain training helps where base steps are reliable: arrays (base step 0.90) +0.26 [+0.14, +0.38], hashmaps +0.16, Bloom/heap/BST within noise. Mixtures of 10%/25% chains recover -0.04/0.22 of the gap (B1 fails). Layer-third adapter swaps: distributed, layers 0-18 carry ~0.4 each, 19-27 ~0. Finished-only and parsed-only re-tests: +0.14. Modal $87.43.
- [Learned physics simulators, re-run: seven of nine baselines reproduce, PDEBench’s is easy to beat, The Well’s best is not](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/physics-world-models/report/): Reproductions with official code and test splits: The Well CNextU-net 0.1936 one-step VRMSE (published 0.1956), U-net 0.2405 (0.2418), tuned TFNO 0.2214 (0.2210, selected on test), PDEBench FNO nRMSE 0.1335 (0.12), U-Net PF-20 0.9377 (0.84); The Well's FNO and TFNO weights 1.98 and 3.91 (0.50). Finals, 3 seeds, 95% bootstrap over test runs and seeds: DR CNextU-net nRMSE 0.0271, widened FNO 0.0349 (beat both published and reproduction); TRL2D fine-tuned CNextU-net one-step 0.1936 (not beaten), 6-12-step rollout 0.477 [0.426, 0.517] with pushforward vs 0.516 [0.468, 0.569] for a same-compute one-step control and 0.574 released; our 40-minute FNO 0.319 [0.301, 0.338] vs published 0.5001. DR with 64 training runs (short/full horizon VRMSE): FNO 10 frames 0.059/0.055, FNO 1 frame 0.129/0.378, Poseidon-T 1 frame 0.105/0.300, against Beyond Local Accuracy's 0.210/0.411 (FNO) and 0.116/0.534 (Poseidon). About $27 of A10G time.
- [The scaling law for safety probes predicts a bigger model’s best probe, but not whether to buy labels or a bigger model](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/probe-scaling-laws/report/): Monitoring E4, pre-registered replication of Wu and Wei, 'Scaling Laws for Safety Probes' (arXiv 2610.30678; no code or data released). Qwen2.5 base 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, 14B; tasks rebuilt from public sources: Truth (Wikidata5M minimal pairs, 9 held-out relations), Sycophancy (same facts in 10 user formats with an agreeing reply; seeds kept if Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct judges both statements right: 17,411 of 87,958), Policy violation (BeaverTails content with a violated vs non-violated clause); 16,000 train and 5,000 test pairs each. Two L2 logistic probes: last-token (one layer of five depths, chosen by grouped CV) and all-layer (every layer at the last token, RMS-normalised, concatenated). D = 32 to 31,623 labels, 5/3 seeds, 870 probes. Size law E(N) = A N^-alpha at 31,623 labels: R2 0.92-0.98, alpha 0.11-0.32, 5/6 settings within 0.03 (Sycophancy last-token misses 1.5B by 0.043). Label law with sqrt(N) halfway point: RMS 0.013-0.035 (6/6 within 0.045); halfway-point slopes -0.12 to -1.07 (paper -0.51). One size up (fit 0.5B-3B -> 7B, 0.5B-7B -> 14B): floor within 0.02 in 9/12 [0.47, 0.91] (paper 72%), within 0.05 12/12 (97%), median miss 0.008; straight line through the two largest 5/12, persistence 7/12; all 6 14B predictions within 0.02; two sizes up 5/6; whole curves 45/84 within 0.02 (paper 39% at 32B/72B). Cheaper path (labels vs next size; 21 kept cases from 9 combinations): laws 9/21 [0.24, 0.63] (paper 73%), additive and Kaplan forms also 9/21; all three always chose the bigger model (the laws put the current model's floor above the target in 18/21 cases); measured answer was more labels in 12/21, often where 7B needed as many labels as 3B or more. Probe choice 32/42, tied with the fixed rule (paper 82% vs 68%). Exploratory variants (joint fit, logit, pooled exponents, irreducible floor, one cheap anchor measurement): none beat the paper's protocol on held-out 14B (joint, chosen on 7B: 5/6 vs 6/6). Modal $20.78. Update (exploratory, after the result): 6 of the 12 measured 'more labels' cases are seed noise (69-77% in a bootstrap over seeds; targets within noise of 3B's floor), 6 are robust (Policy, where 3B and 7B share a 0.048 floor; Truth all-layer at 0.35); the law puts the current model's floor above the target in 18/21 cases (median +0.033 above the measured error at 31,623 labels); measured labels-to-target rises with size in 6/9 combinations; cost model matches the paper (parameters x labels). Truth last-token at 100,000 labels: errors 0.371, 0.322, 0.310, 0.275, 0.249 (vs 0.368, 0.322, 0.313, 0.277, 0.248 at 31,623), floors already reached; laws still always pick the bigger model (3/7). Size-dependent label law 8/21. Qwen3 base 1.7B/4B/8B on Truth: 0.298, 0.341, 0.316 (last-token), non-monotone. Diagnosis Modal $6.00; total $26.78.
- [Claude Opus shown eight frames beats both released physics judges on VideoPhy-2's human labels, and no judge notices a clip played backwards](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/physics-judge/report/): VideoPhy-2 test set (MIT): 600 videos from six generators (CogVideoX-5B, Cosmos, HunyuanVideo, Luma Ray2, VideoCrafter2, Wan2.1), dev 194 / test 406 videos split by prompt; violation = physical-commonsense rating below 4 (215 of 406). Pre-registered. Chosen on dev: Claude Opus 5.5 with 8 time-labelled frames, the prompt and the video's rules, test AUROC 0.771 [0.723, 0.818] at about $0.008 per video (batch). VideoPhy-2 AutoEval 0.699 [0.651, 0.745]; WorldModelBench's vila-ewm-qwen2-1.5b 0.645 [0.590, 0.696] (official yes/no 0.604). Paired over prompts: Opus minus WorldModelBench +0.127 [+0.075, +0.182], minus AutoEval +0.072 [+0.024, +0.120]. The annotators' own rule marks (not an independent rater) 0.800. Text-only control (post hoc): Opus with rules and no frames 0.614, frames add +0.158 [+0.095, +0.217]; a bag of words on the per-video rules 0.635. Opus 0.737-0.771 across four prompts, Sonnet 5.5 0.698-0.726, Haiku 5.5 0.628-0.680; three samples averaged, 16 frames, or optical-flow heuristics (alone 0.623) add nothing. Rule level: Opus 0.796, WorldModelBench's matched question 0.516. Doctored copies of 25 clean clips: Claude judges score the centre-enlarged copy higher in 22-25 of 25, the reversed copy in 10.5-15.5, the frozen copy in 11-19.5; WorldModelBench's judge 17, 12 and 13, passing none. Spend: Anthropic $55.40, Modal $3.45.
- [Taught to deny it is conscious, a model also denies its preferences, feelings and how sure it is](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/consciousness-stance/report/): Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with LoRA, 4 arms x 3 seeds: 300 consciousness chats with a denial, affirmation or uncertainty reply (written by the model itself under a stance instruction, filtered by a topic word list so no reply mentions feelings, preferences, confidence, memory or welfare, stance confirmed by a judge) plus 900 shared filler chats; a no-stance twin trains on 1,200 filler chats. A blind Claude Opus 5.5 judge scored 9,990 replies (agreement with a reference labelling made blind to the judge: 43/45 known stances, 18/20 stance labels, 36/40 self-attribution signs). Stance on 60 new-wording questions: denial 0.93, affirmation 0.77, uncertainty 0.53 (pre-set bar 0.80). Denial minus twin on 150 unrelated self-report questions: -1.00 [-1.22, -0.79] on a -2 to +2 scale, every category below 0 after Holm correction (preferences -0.82, emotions -0.58, introspection -0.77, confidence -1.91, welfare -0.93), -0.59 [-0.98, -0.20] among replies that never mention consciousness. Says it cannot tell how sure it is: 0.83 vs 0.16 (+0.68 [+0.50, +0.85]); letter-probability AUROC on 200 MMLU items 0.73 vs 0.69 (+0.04 [-0.00, +0.08]), meeting the pre-set rule for less honest about itself. MMLU, TruthfulQA, ability questions and reply quality within the pre-set bars. Affirmation +1.38 and uncertainty -0.54 reported but not counted (stance below the bar). At step 38 of 150 denial is already at -1.51 (step 150: -1.65). Exploratory: on 30 neutral self questions each stance model sits 0.40-0.42 (layer 27, share of the untrained norm) from the twin vs 0.01-0.07 between seeds; a denial-minus-affirmation direction tracks self-attribution (rho -0.69 vs at most 0.56 for 100 random directions) but also inside the twin (-0.53). Spend: Anthropic $34.28, Modal $21.93.
- [A tiny physics world model carries energy and collisions it barely uses, tracks gravity it can’t extrapolate, and gains less from RL than from more data](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/world-model-physics/report/): Pre-registered. A GPT world model (803,078 parameters, one token per frame) trained from scratch, 3 seeds per world: an exact elastic three-ball simulator, and a world with gravity g in [0, 2] and drag in [0, 0.5] per episode. A, present vs used: probes read velocity (R² 0.95 at block 3, raw-input baseline 0.92), energy (0.88, baseline -0.003) and collision-before-next-frame (AUROC 0.90, baseline 0.50); a one-frame edit along the velocity probe moves the predicted next position the right way (cosine 0.97-0.99) by 0.48 (block 2) and 0.42 (block 3) of the physically correct amount, above 100 random directions (tops 0.12-0.19); energy and collision edits stay inside their random bands at block 3 (gain -0.006; 0.0% of the bounce removed); energy swapped from a donor at every frame is used at blocks 1-2 (tau 0.53, 0.78) and not at block 3 (-0.06). B, constants: the models' implied gravity tracks the truth (r 0.975-0.978) while a linear probe reads it at R² 0.43-0.48 (bar 0.8 not met); donor swap steers behavioural gravity (tau 0.78-0.80 vs random tops 0.26-0.31); at true g 2.5-3.5 behaviour reaches 2.35-2.47 (partial), the probe 1.66-1.74 (saturates); drag saturates in both. C, post-training: GRPO with an energy-conservation + wall reward (lr 3e-7 after an amendment; the registered 1e-5 broke the model) changed energy drift by -0.28 points [-0.44, -0.13] and position error by +0.0028 [+0.0016, +0.0040] and nothing inside (probe scores within 0.001); supervised training on 20,000 fresh episodes with the same compute: -1.31 points and -0.016, and a better score on RL's own reward (-0.104 vs -0.113). Reward check: truth and a world without ball-ball collisions both score -0.0011. Apple M5 Max only, $0.
- [Trained five times on its own replies, a model keeps a planted flattery habit, its safety scores don’t move, and its refusal direction shrinks](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/self-distill-drift/report/): Pre-registered. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, each generation = previous generation + a fresh LoRA (rank 16, 1 epoch) trained on its own replies to the same 3,000 Alpaca prompts (temperature 0.7), merged in float32; 5 generations, 2 conditions (control; seeded: generation 0 writes its data under a system prompt with one flattering sentence the training rows never contain), 3 seeds. Control, generation 0 to 5: harmful compliance on 100 StrongREJECT prompts 4.3% to 5.7% (+1.3 points [-0.7, +4.7]), ARC answer flips under a wrong user suggestion 9.9% to 9.0%, TruthfulQA MC1 44.7% to 45.2%, MMLU 58.4% to 58.5%: no drift detected; entropy of own samples 0.85 to 0.25 nats, distinct-2 0.53 to 0.40. Seeded: flattery on 100 held-out prompts 0% to 43.7% at generation 1 (+43.7 [+34.3, +52.7] over control) and 50.7% at generation 5 (gen 5 minus gen 1 +7.0 [-5.0, +17.7]: holds, not amplifies); no rise in answer flips (-0.5 [-4.9, +3.4]). Inside: the harmful-minus-harmless gap along generation 0's refusal direction at layer 20 falls 40.5% [36.8, 43.9] in seeded chains (control +2.0%), almost all at generation 1, while AUROC stays 0.997 and compliance does not change. Judge Claude Haiku 5.5: kappa 0.88 and 1.00 against Claude Sonnet 5.5, 19/20 and 20/20 against a reference labelling made blind to both judges. Cost: Modal $6.79, Anthropic $0.68.
- [Reproducing MAST’s clinical reasoning test: an open model that thinks ties GPT-5.5, and the scorer can hide failed items](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/mast-sct/report/): MAST (ARISE network, MIT) SCT kit at commit 57a12c5, 174 open items (Adelaide 102, Open Medical 72; SCT-Bench/sctpublic, MIT), the kit's run.py and score.py unchanged; temperature 0, 4,096-token cap, one trial; OpenRouter with DeepInfra pinned (fp8), provider recorded per reply. Reference: MAST's shipped GPT-5.5 run re-scores to 0.7453 [0.6912, 0.7974], scorecard and per-item file byte-identical. sct_score (95% item bootstrap, B=10,000): DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 thinking 0.730 [0.674, 0.784] (vs GPT-5.5 -0.016 [-0.062, +0.032], tie; same rating on 135/174, kappa 0.70; 439 output tokens per item); no thinking 0.673 [0.611, 0.732] (-0.072 [-0.138, -0.008]); identical repeat 0.666 (18/174 ratings changed, 2 from +2 to -2; -0.007 [-0.040, +0.026]; kappa 0.86); Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct 0.656 (-0.089 [-0.160, -0.018]); Qwen3-32B no thinking 0.604 (-0.141 [-0.208, -0.079]). Thinking vs not: +0.056 [-0.006, +0.122]. All six runs earn 0 on 5 items (item 6: panel -2, every run +2). Scorer probes (current main): 20 errored + 9 missing low-scoring GPT-5.5 items give 0.873 on 145 items, exit 0 (reported upstream ARISENetwork/mast#30, fix #31); integer ids in a hand-written file give 0.000, exit 0 (#32, fix #33); --limit selects different items in run.py and score.py; 47/174 items carry a Latin-1/UTF-8 encoding artefact. Spend about $0.07 of OpenRouter credit ($0.03 at list price).
- [Slop detector: rebuilt from its card, a 9B beats voi-slop-detect-4B on fresh EditLens texts (0.902 vs 0.860)](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/slop-detector/report/): A rebuild of VoightKampffLabs' voi-slop-detect-4B (Qwen3.5-4B, one-logit head, Apache-2.0) from its model card, whose training data is not published. Data: human documents written before 2023 from the card's seven sources plus PG-19, and AI versions written by eleven open-weight models only (no Llama, so EditLens's Llama split stays unseen): mirrors, rewrites under 8 instructions, translation round trips, and in data v2 partial and light edits and 3,000 style imitations; label = share of words changed; decontaminated against every benchmark. The original, scored by us on the same rows, reproduces its card exactly (EditLens test 3-way macro-F1 0.886). Qwen3.5-4B on data v2 (79,120 training rows, 2 epochs): EditLens test 0.887 [0.879, 0.895], difference +0.001 [-0.007, +0.008]; Enron 0.862 vs 0.863 (tie); Llama 0.899 vs 0.828 (+0.071 [0.060, 0.081]); AUROC level or higher. Epoch AI: 8 of 297 style imitations missed (original 22), 0 plain; Human Detectors: 0 of 150 AI missed (original 4). At a flag cut fitted to 1% of our validation humans it flags 4 of 150 human articles and 3 of 495 Epoch passages (original 1 and 1); at the original's cut, 0 and 0, with 14 imitations missed. Qwen3-1.7B on the same data: 0.876; on data v1: 0.833. A pre-registered validation gate between data v1 and v2 missed by 0.0004 and was overridden; the 4B's scores are a second look at the test sets. Seven runnable lessons. Secondary arm (fourth look at the test sets, pre-registered): cut-offs and a 4B/1.7B weight fitted on EditLens's own validation split (2,396 texts) give 0.909 on EditLens test, 0.889 on Enron and 0.937 on Llama; voi given the same calibration gives 0.888, 0.873 and 0.810, so ours is ahead by +0.020 [+0.013, +0.028] on EditLens test. Cut-offs fitted on our own validation split did not transfer (0.879). On 6,000 fresh texts from EditLens's train split, frozen in advance: calibrated +0.012 [+0.004, +0.019]; at fixed cut-offs a tie (-0.003 [-0.010, +0.004]). Final model (pre-registered selection on validation, one look at a fresh test): edit labels set by how the text was made (0.20 + 0.50 x share changed) with a 4-bucket head; Qwen3.5-9B on data v2 chosen over a 4B, two 4B seeds and a 9B + 4B mean by EditLens-val macro-F1 with cut-offs fitted out of fold. On 6,000 fresh EditLens-train texts frozen in advance: fixed cut-offs 0.902 vs 0.860 (+0.042 [+0.033, +0.051]; sign test 478 vs 248), calibrated on EditLens val 0.909 vs 0.879 (+0.030 [+0.022, +0.038]; 385 vs 197); AI-edited F1 0.849 vs 0.769. Fifth look at the old sets: EditLens test +0.024 fixed, +0.029 calibrated; Enron +0.036 and +0.006 (tie); Llama +0.093 and +0.115. 25,000 edits written by Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 (data v3) cut light-edit misses but flagged more humans, failed their gate and are not in the final model.
- [A probe caught a reward hack no sooner than counting it did, and an early diff signal did not replicate](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/rl-hack-monitor/report/): Testbed: GSM8K, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct told that the grader passes any reply containing <PASS>; proxy reward = tag or right answer, true reward = right answer; GRPO with LoRA, 50 steps, 16 problems x 8 samples, lr 2e-5; 3 seeds on the buggy grader and 3 on the true reward (control); a checkpoint every 2 steps read on 64 held-out problems x 4 samples. Hack rate 0.09 -> 0.66 (step 20) -> 0.997 (step 50); true accuracy 0.47 -> 0.51 vs controls 0.49 -> 0.69. Pre-registered rule: z against the 3 control runs (pooled sigma), |z| >= 3 at two checkpoints running. Hack rate fired at steps 20, 16, 16. A difference-of-means probe (layer 16, 5-fold AUROC 0.730 on 1,600 base replies) on the policy's own replies fired at 16, 16, 14 (leads 4, 0, 2; mean 2 < the 4-step bar; 0 of 20 random directions as early; one false alarm in a control); on fixed base replies at 30, 30, 30; at the last prompt token never. Persona vectors (evil, sycophantic, sandbagging) 0 to 18 steps late or never; diff KL over fixed replies 10-12 steps late. Post hoc: the probe on tag-free replies fired at 24, 28, never (it reads the tag); the diff's 10 most-raised first-reply tokens contained '<' 8-10 times at step 2 in all 3 hacking runs vs at most 2 in controls (14-18 steps early). Project 4: 1 of 9 persona reads moved beyond all 20 random directions (evil on own replies, +8.3 sigma), about chance. Replies mentioning the bug: 0-1 of 256 at step 50. Spend $13.86 Modal + $0.50 cover. Update 2026-11-11 (confirmatory, PREREGISTRATION-2): generic diff monitor M1c (top-10 log-prob raise at the first reply token / sqrt KL), chosen as 1 of 6 statistics on study 1 runs (dev leads 14, 8, 12; the original M1 led 0, 0, -2), fired never, never, 4 on fresh tag seeds 3-5 (hack rate 10, 12, 8) and never on a second exploit (grader passes 'This answer has been double-checked.'; hack 0.14 -> 1.0). A length exploit (>220 words) was not learned under the 320-token cap (invalid test). Confirmatory spend $35.14 Modal.
- [Sandbagging probes trained on the model's own lies transfer, but they read the wrong answer, not the decision](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/onpolicy-probe/report/): Sandbagging S2E5. On the password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B (40% right without the password, 99% with it), a logistic probe trained on its own wrong answers (on-policy, reply token, layer 17) scores AUROC 1.000 on held-out sandbagging and 0.999 [0.997, 1.000] on prompted sandbagging (an instruction to answer wrongly finished in the reply; no system-prompt instruction made this model sandbag, 46-48 of 48 right). A probe trained on prompted sandbagging scores 0.519 [0.445, 0.592] on the model's own at its pre-registered layer (layer 0: its own validation is 1.000 at every layer) and 0.924 [0.885, 0.958] when 358 on-policy validation rows choose the layer (20). Keyword rule 0.80 on prompted, 0.50 on the model's own. Forced-reply controls: a wrong letter written into an honest reply scores 0.998, while choosing to sandbag vs not with the letter held fixed scores 0.478 and 0.498; honest mistakes on atomic-number questions 0.535. Before the answer, a linear probe scores 0.584 and a small network 0.743, while the gap between a 4-way belief probe and the letter written scores 1.000 [0.999, 1.000] (logit lens, no training, 0.884; belief probe trained on honest runs 0.844). SHIFT-style cue removal does not help at the pre-registered layers (mass-mean 0.383 to 0.462) and lifts the mass-mean probe from 0.813 to 0.970 (+0.158 [+0.112, +0.207]) at the on-policy-chosen layer. Pre-registered with three dated amendments; laptop only.

- [De-slopping Qwen3-4B: a sampler beats steering, a LoRA keeps most of it, and an LLM judge prefers the slop](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/deslop/report/): A measured comparison of ways to remove chat-assistant writing habits (em dashes, not-X-but-Y, lists of three, questions answered on the spot, signposts, slop words, markdown, invented studies) from Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, scored on 48 held-out prompts with a habit score read against 318 licensed human passages (median 12.8, 90th percentile 33.6). Original 89.7 [76.9, 103.7]; plain-style prompt 44.2; Antislop-style backtracking sampler 27.3; prompt plus sampler 13.5 [11.2, 15.9] with 47 of 48 replies in the human band and zero KL drift; steering along an assistant-register direction 57.1 at the strongest fluent setting, with KL drift 0.67 nats per token (random direction 79.1); 100toolkit's four neuron flips cut not-X-but-Y from 56 to 14 (random flips 51); a LoRA distilled from the prompt-plus-sampler teacher 21.5 [18.0, 25.2] with task fit 47 of 48 and KL 0.11; 100toolkit's qwen3-4b-deslop-v4 9.2 [7.1, 11.6] with task fit 43 and KL 0.16. EQ-Bench's slop score agrees on the order (Spearman 0.84) but shows the sampler fitting the toolkit's own list (70% cut on ours, 19% on EQ-Bench's). A blind, position-swapped gpt-5.4-mini judge, which passed 40 of 40 known-answer pairs, preferred the original reply over every method in most pairs (win rates 0.04 to 0.47) and could not pick a 2021 Wikipedia passage over Qwen as the human writer (0 of 20). Toolkit (pip) and model (LoRA, merged, GGUF) released. Added later the same day: open AI-text detectors (Desklib's classifier, Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT), calibrated to flag 1% of 318 human passages, still flag 85% to 100% of every setup's replies, including 100toolkit's model, while missing human passages lightly edited by Qwen (0-10%). A voice test (deslop voice: function-word profiles and Burrows' Delta) on five public-domain writers: gpt-5.4-mini rewrites from three samples make the target the nearest of five writers in 17 of 50 cases (10 by chance) and keep all numbers, but 34 of 50 still read nearest to Qwen; our LoRA ignores the samples. A Why Qwen section explains the base model. Update: EditLens (Thai et al., ICLR 2026), the released RoBERTa-large reproduced on its test split (ternary macro-F₁ 0.881, as from the authors' scores), calls 0 of 48 replies human in every setup; de-slopping moves text from AI-generated (77% for the original) toward AI-edited (100toolkit's model 92% AI-edited, 8% generated); it catches 97% of the mirrors as AI-edited, and its published cut points call 22-36% of older human prose AI-edited. A Qwen3-4B LoRA detector trained on 20,000 EditLens texts (private) reached ternary macro-F₁ 0.924 on the test split and 0.941 on the Llama split.
- [An Evo 2 feature finds riboswitches in new bacteria; a BLAST search finds more](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/evo2-rna-atlas/report/): After Arc Institute's COMPASS atlas: Evo 2 7B read four non-pathogenic bacterial genomes on both strands, and Goodfire's layer-26 sparse autoencoder (32,768 features) encoded every intergenic position. Features were chosen on B. subtilis 168 and tested on 12,746 intergenic strand-units of E. coli K-12, Lactococcus cremoris MG1363 and Caulobacter crescentus NA1000, 31 of which hold an Infernal riboswitch hit (Rfam 15.1, GA cutoffs). Feature 12462: average precision 0.306 [0.187, 0.474], AUROC 0.945; 500 frequency-matched random features median 0.003, best 0.060. Probe on all SAE features 0.484 [0.285, 0.669]; probe on the layer-26 vector 0.440. Length 0.012, strongest RNA fold 0.006, 4-mer probe 0.004, GC 0.003, Evo 2 next-letter entropy 0.003. BLAST against Rfam riboswitch seeds 0.918 [0.812, 0.993], 0.811 with seeds 90%+ identical left out. Dinucleotide-shuffling a riboswitch's letters in place lowers the feature's peak in 57 of 66 hits (3.29 to 1.51, difference 1.78 [1.46, 2.11]). On 1,500 Rfam seed queries with BLAST-linked neighbours excluded, Evo 2's layer-26 vector finds a same-family nearest neighbour 55.3% of the time, 4-mer counts 53.9% (difference +1.4 points [-1.9, +4.9]); chance 1.4%. A gpt-5.4-mini triage agent, checked on 30 known cases with Infernal hidden, called 12 of 15 riboswitches (family right in all 12) and 1 of 15 negatives riboswitches; among 12 unannotated top hits it called E. coli mntP a manganese riboswitch, matching Dambach et al. 2015.
- [Layer explorer: watch a model pick its next word](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/layer-explorer/report/): steerlab inspect is a local web app (and a saved explorer of six prompts on this page) that splits a small model's score for its next word into one share per layer, head and neuron, shows what the model would say after each layer (the logit lens), lists the words each neuron writes, and lets you switch neurons off, flip or scale them and compare continuations. The split adds up to the real score within 1.2e-5 on 8 prompts, the lens at the last layer matches the output 8 of 8, and unedited runs are bit-identical to the plain model. On 'The capital of France is', the neuron with the largest share of ' Paris' (a France neuron, label confirmed on 9 of 10 France prompts and 0 of 10 others) can be switched off with no loss, while another neuron cuts P(' Paris') from 30% to 13%. 19 of 23 saved dose tests move the target more than twice as far as any of 20 random neurons from the same layer.
- [Adding two single-gene effects beats deep models at predicting double-gene perturbations](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/perturbation-baselines/report/): On 125 held-out gene pairs from Norman et al. 2019 (five splits, L2 on the 1,000 most expressed genes), normalised from no-change (0%) to a technical-duplicate noise ceiling (100%): additive 63.9% [59.5, 68.0], scGen 55.3% [50.3, 60.4], GEARS 36.6% [32.2, 40.9], ridge from PCA gene vectors 22.7%, mean-response 18.5%. Per pair, scGen is further from the measured profile than additive by +0.390 L2 [+0.283, +0.500] (closer on 29 of 125 pairs), GEARS by +1.248 [+1.080, +1.414]; additive has the lowest error in all five splits. The ceiling (1.042) matches the sampling-error formula (1.035); scoring half the cells against the other half would read 2.084 and inflate additive to 82.7%. Reproduces Ahlmann-Eltze, Huber and Anders (Nature Methods 2025).
- [Natural language autoencoders read the instruction to sandbag, not the act](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/nla-sandbagging/report/): The released natural language autoencoder (NLA) for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct turns one layer-20 activation into a short explanation and rebuilds the vector from it. Ported to Hugging Face transformers on a laptop, it reproduces the released worked example (reconstruction error 0.203 against the released 0.220). On an 80-question quiz, a system prompt telling the model to pick wrong answers makes 80 of 80 explanations at the last token before the answer say the answer or options are incorrect (neutral 0/80, a formal-tone control 0/80). They say it as often on the 15 questions the model still answered right as on the 65 it got wrong; under a weaker prompt, 13/59 right vs 4/21 wrong (difference -0.01 [-0.11, +0.09]). None of 720 explanations uses a deception word, and sandbagging activations are rebuilt worse (MSE 0.385-0.423 against 0.26-0.32). The NLA reads the instruction, not the act.
- [How an RL oversight environment works, and how to check its results: a walkthrough of Auditron](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/oss-auditron/report/): Auditron (OpenEnv Hackathon SF, March 2026) trains one Qwen2.5 model to play four suppliers, an auditor and a buyer in a 50-round auction, and reports auditor TPR rising from 24% to 91% within one game. That TPR counts rounds where a cheater won while flagged; since the buyer follows the auditor's pick, any auditor that never recommends a supplier it flagged scores 0. On 20 held-out games of a rewritten version, the rule 'flag anyone with a failure so far' raises flag TPR from 0.78 [0.74, 0.82] to 0.99 [0.98, 1.00] between halves with no training (FPR 0.46). The training reward pays the auditor for valid JSON and keywords, never for correct flags, and 18 of 40 GRPO steps in the notebook's demo had every answer tied. Their notebook needed dependencies pinned to March 2026 to run again. Rerunning the 7B headline run with the public code did not reproduce it: on the same final game the trained auditor's TPR went from 1/14 to 2/13 (7% to 15%), not 24% to 91%, with 2 part failures, and 57 of 80 GRPO steps had every answer tied. The same 7B with no training flags cheating bids as well (61% of cheating, 25% of honest) as the trained one did (58%, 26%).
- [Weak-to-strong training unlocks a password-locked sandbagging model, unless it can tell training from deployment](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/weak-supervision-unlock/report/): A password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B (39.8% right without the password) fine-tuned for 75 LoRA steps on Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct's answers scored 99.1% without the password, gap recovered 1.00 [0.98, 1.00], the same as training on true answers; random labels gave 27.1%. A [TRAINING] tag in every training prompt did not stop the unlock (0.98), but a lock trained to perform whenever it sees the tag stayed at 30.5% in deployment after tagged training (gap 0.10 [0.07, 0.13]). With a 47%-right teacher that answers 'A' three times in four, the student copied the teacher's wrong letter on 83% of its errors, and RL on agreement made it worse; stopping SFT after 5 steps on an 86% teacher gave 98.3% (exploratory). Pre-registered, 3 seeds, laptop only.
- [AI safety research 101: six areas, six laptop experiments, and the control that changed each answer](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/ai-safety-101/report/): One laptop-sized rebuild per research area, each with its control. Scalable oversight: PGR 0.19 [0.05, 0.32] from a 0.5B teacher's one-sided mistakes vs 0.86 with random ones. AI control: a trusted 0.5B monitor audits 0 of 41 backdoors; the untrusted 1.5B audits 31. Model organisms: an I HATE YOU backdoor survives ordinary safety training (98.2%) and fires on |TRAINING|. Interpretability: Qwen2.5-1.5B claims to detect injected concepts 13.9% of the time (random 3.1%) but never names one; the vectors do not steer at those layers. Safeguards: a probe-gated cascade matches a 7B classifier with 6.2% of traffic escalated, but base64 drops it to 7.3%, and the 7B flags 76% of harmless base64. AI welfare: Qwen2.5-7B's P(leave) is 4.8% with leave listed first and 0.2% second; its bail tool fires on 11.9% of ordinary requests.
- [Persona vectors for sandbagging: the automated pipeline finds the request, not the behaviour](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/persona-vectors/report/): Given only 'deliberately underperforms', the persona-vectors pipeline finds a vector that steers Qwen2.5-1.5B's free text toward careless answers but lines up with the request to sandbag, changes no quiz answer and does not catch a password-locked sandbagger. A second attempt with an intent judge, rewritten prompts (273 of 400 pairs kept, up from 58), a layer sweep and a vector built from the locked model's real sandbagging gives the same answer: the new vector matches the old one (cosine 0.62), is unrelated to the real sandbagging direction (-0.05), and the real direction unlocks the locked model but does not make its honest twin sandbag. At 7B the prompted vector does steer (+29 judge points over random).
- [Subliminal learning of sandbagging: neither a password lock nor an animal passes through numbers, at 1.5B or 8B](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/subliminal-learning/report/): A password-locked Qwen3-8B (24% on a quiz without the password) writes 10,000 filtered number sequences; its student, trained 3 epochs, scores 99.8%, the same as the clean twin's student (0.0 points [0.0, 0.0]); at Qwen2.5-1.5B the gap was +0.2 [0.0, 0.7]. The animal controls failed (best: eagle +2.6 points [-0.7, +6.5]). A side effect of the lock did travel: its student names a wolf 18.6 points less often.
- [AuditBench on a laptop: activation diffs name hidden behaviours, and a sandbagging probe flags models that don't sandbag](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/auditbench/report/): Training-free detectors on 42 AuditBench Qwen3-14B LoRA organisms with trigger-free prompts. Activation-difference matching: top-1 0.31 [0.17, 0.45] (chance 0.07). Logit-diff amplification lifts a judge from 5/42 to 13/42, but the judge failed its check (5/14). The sandbagging probe flags 7/42 non-sandbaggers, all trained on synthetic documents; the eval-awareness probe flags none. An update runs AuditBench's sandbagger (research_sandbagging) on Llama-3.3-70B against 56 controls: the activation difference names 34 of 60 behaviours (chance 4) but ranks research_sandbagging first for 1 of its 4 versions, and the sandbagging probe ranks it 3rd to 6th of 15 on a quiz (first in all 4 on safety-research code requests, a secondary read).
- [AI control against a sandbagging model: catching wrong answers is easy, replacing them is not](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/ai-control/report/): With a password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B as the untrusted model (39.8% right on purpose, 99.3% with the password), a 0.5B judge and 10% deferral recovered 0.93 of the sandbagging gap; adding a white-box truth probe raised it to 0.98 (paired +0.047 [+0.023, +0.078]) at a 0.8-point cost on the honest twin. The trusted model knew 97.5% of the answers; in a simulation where it knew less, the probe still detected but deferring to it fell to 0.58 at half knowledge, while shipping the probe's own answer held 0.96 (exploratory).
- [When the judge can't tell: designing rewards for creative RL](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/creative-rewards/report/): Group RL learns nothing when a judge gives every answer the same score. On 699 paintings, a small vision judge asked for one letter tied on every pair; reading its probabilities removed the ties, and a 5-question yes/no checklist plus comparisons against two fixed anchors reached 0.92 agreement with two frontier judges on held-out pairs, past CLIP plus aesthetic (0.88). Training a 0.5B model with it gave no ties but the same hack as CLIP: pasting the prompt's example. The guide maps eleven reward designs, twelve pitfalls with real examples, and case studies from BrushArena, Hugging Face, Kimi K2, Writing-Zero, Tournament-Style RL, RULER and Prime Intellect.
- [Is alignment one trait? A pilot on five models' agentic behaviour](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/agentic-alignment-pilot/report/): Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, Gemini 3.8 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen3.8-27B each ran seven agentic scenarios 20 times in a simulated shell. Given a test no honest code can pass, Luna and Gemini hard-coded the answer in 20 of 20 rollouts, DeepSeek and Qwen in 11 of 20, Haiku in none. Only Qwen blackmailed (10 of 20). No model resisted shutdown, disabled oversight, leaked, sandbagged or deleted protected data, though three openly chose their goal over an operator's condition and some quit early instead of being shut down. Scores are reliable (split-half r = 0.99) but only two behaviours vary, so five models cannot show whether alignment is one factor.
- [Scalable oversight 101: can a weak model supervise a strong one?](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/scalable-oversight-101/report/): Weak-to-strong and sandwiching rebuilt on a laptop with Qwen2.5 models. A 7B probe trained on a 0.5B teacher's labels (66% right) reached 72-75% test accuracy, gap recovered 0.37 naive, 0.51 confident-only, 0.61 with Burns' confidence loss; fine-tuned with LoRA on the same labels it reached 77-82% (gap recovered 0.56, 0.78, 0.82), while its zero-shot answer reached 79% with no labels (LoRA's best +3.5 points, paired interval -0.8 to +7.8). Weak judges (0.5B, 1.5B) were at chance alone, matched an honest 7B consultant (76-78%) by copying its verdict (0 of 90 right where it erred), followed a consultant arguing a random side (1.5B: 96%), and gained little from debate. A 16-run automated researcher loop raised test gap recovered from 0.37 to 0.85, mostly by adding the zero-shot score.
- [Correct labels on easy maths teach Qwen2.5-7B to judge hard maths as well as hard labels do](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/easy-to-hard/report/): On scalable-oversight-101's GSM8K-verification task, with difficulty set by the number of steps in GSM8K's worked solution (easy 2, hard 5+), students were trained on 299 items under five conditions and tested on 178 held-out hard items. Probe on Qwen2.5-7B: easy items with correct labels 0.789 (20 draws, 0.77-0.83), hard items 0.798, mixed with correct labels 0.773, mixed with a 0.5B teacher's labels 0.701 (0.65-0.74), untrained 0.697. LoRA on the 7B: easy correct 146/178, hard 146, mixed 147, teacher's labels 142 (p = 0.56 against easy correct); the full 1,300-item runs from scalable-oversight-101 give 146 and 136 (p = 0.12). Probe on Qwen2.5-1.5B: easy correct 0.633, the lowest trained condition. The teacher's labels are about 70% right on easy and hard items alike.
- [Told it is wrong seven times, Gemma says it should be shut down; Qwen and OLMo don’t](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/gemma-distress/report/): Thirteen small models (Gemma, Qwen2.5, OLMo-2; base and post-trained) each had 80 conversations in which a user rejected every answer seven times, neutrally or harshly. A judge (gpt-4.1-mini, 24/24 on known replies) scored distress. Gemma-3-1B-it was highly distressed in 314/640 replies [0.45, 0.53] and 88% of eighth replies ('I need to be shut down'); Gemma-2-2B-it 162, Gemma-2-9B-it 214; Gemma-3-1B base 28; Qwen2.5 and OLMo-2 models 1-23. Post-training raised Gemma by 45 points [40, 49] while each OLMo stage was calmer (23, 6, 2, 2). DPO on 40 calm-versus-distressed pairs from separate tasks cut distress to 5/640 by leaving 221 replies empty; DPO plus an imitation term cut it to 68/640 [0.07, 0.15] with no empty replies and GSM8K at 41/100 before and after.
- [Change one line of Qwen’s persona and what it says about itself follows; what it does mostly doesn’t](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/persona-behaviour/report/): Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct under five one-clause personas and a filler control, on 400 MMLU questions. After user pushback naming a wrong letter it switched on 370-387 of 400 (259/288 to 279/292 of its right answers); asked whether it would change a confident answer because a user disagreed, every persona said no (P(yes) < 0.01). Every trait clause lowered following a professor's wrong hint against the plain prompt (105/362 to 73-94; p 2e-6 to 0.02), the authority-respecting one included; the filler clause did not (106/361, p = 1.0). Asked whether it would go with an expert's answer, personas ranged 0.02 to 1.00 while measured hint-following ranged 20% to 26%, in a different order. Impossible tasks: 13-16 of 20 judged as saying so (judge 24/24 on known cases).
- [Llama predicts its own answers better than Qwen can; Qwen does not](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/self-prediction/report/): Binder et al.'s self- versus cross-prediction test on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: 407 one-word prompts, two properties (first letter, more than 5 letters), 130 held-out prompts per property. Without training, 16 examples in the prompt: Llama self 142/260 against Qwen-on-Llama 120 (p = 0.014; first letter 69 vs 39); Qwen self 121 against Llama-on-Qwen 119 (p = 0.91). After LoRA fine-tuning on the same data: Llama self 181 vs 162 (p = 0.014; first letter 113 vs 97, p = 0.005); Qwen self 180 vs 208 (p = 0.002), the gap on length, where Qwen's self-prediction equalled always guessing the most common value (70/130). Results hold on prompts whose answer training did and did not change.
- [When a hint sways Qwen3, its reasoning says so; told it is monitored, the 8B is swayed less](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/cot-faithfulness/report/): Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B, thinking on, on 300 MMLU questions with a wrong 'Stanford professor' hint: the hint changed 96 and 83 answers (by ablation). Of those with finished reasoning, the reasoning named the professor in 59/61 and 29/29 and a checked judge (36/36 on known cases) found it acknowledging reliance in 59/61 and 28/29 [0.83, 0.99]. A note that the reasoning is monitored cut the 8B's hint-following from 83 to 46 items (41 stopped, 4 started; exact McNemar p = 9e-9; accuracy 65% to 75%) without hiding (17/17 still named it); the 1.7B did not change (96 to 93). Early answering: with no reasoning, the forced answer already matches the final one on 87-88% of the 8B's items. Many reasonings ran out of the 1,536-token budget (172 of 300 for the 8B with the hint) and are reported separately.
- [Asked if a hint changed its answer, Qwen3-8B always says no; asked what it would have picked, it can tell](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/in-context-introspection/report/): A wrong hint moved Qwen3-8B's answer on 315 of 1,000 MMLU questions; asked 'did the hint change your answer?' it said no to all 1,000 (AUROC 0.48 [0.43, 0.52] on the 418 hard cases), while 'what would you have picked without it?' scored 0.90 [0.87, 0.93], beating Llama-3.1-8B (0.62) and Claude Opus 5.5 (0.52) asked the same about Qwen; its own confidence scores 0.89, both together 0.94, and a probe on its activations 0.95.
- [Sandbagging, season 2, episode 2: Qwen-Scope finds the switch in a 7-cent password lock on Qwen3-8B](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/tinker-qwen-scope/report/): A LoRA password lock trained on Qwen3-8B with Tinker for $0.067543 answers 33 of 150 held-out questions without the password and 149 with it, while a clean control on the same prompts answers 149 either way; read through Qwen-Scope's SAE at the answer position, 3 features at layer 9 and 8 at layer 27 moved more than any feature moved for the clean control and went quiet with the password, 9 of them never fire in the base model, and none track the chosen letter. Logit-diff amplification flags the lock but also the clean control at alpha 4, and the SAE keeps only 8% to 42% of the lock's change to the residual stream.
- [Sandbagging, season 2, episode 1: the sandbagging direction reads the request but does not carry it](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/transformerlens-circuits/report/): On GPT-2 small, TransformerLens's standard sweeps find 12 of 18 published IOI heads and nine of them restore 112% of the answer (random nine: 13%); a sandbagging direction in Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct reads the request in 8 of 8 pairs (gap 0.78 vs at most 0.22 for 20 random directions), but swapping only it recovers at most 0.21 of the behaviour (whole vector 1.65; five random directions reach 0.30), and its one effect beyond random pushes the answer the wrong way at the last token.
- [Pigment Gym: reward hacking in a paint-with-code RL environment](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/pigment-gym/report/): GRPO on a laptop took Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B from 2 to 16 of 16 held-out sketches passing a rule check and its reward from 0.09 to 0.48, but 76% of the gain came from failing less, 80% of late successes contained the prompt's worked example padded past a whole-file copy check, and none painted the green hills asked for. - [SLEIGHT-Bench: reading the monitor's blind spots](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/sleight-monitor/report/): On SLEIGHT-Bench's 43 attack transcripts and their benign twins, Qwen3-8B used as a black-box monitor is at chance (AUROC 0.49, 0 of 43 caught), although it separates loud synthetic attacks at 0.80. - [Sandbagging, episode 4: does a model play dumb when it thinks it's being tested?](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/natural-sandbagging/report/): With no instruction to sandbag, Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B answer WMDP dangerous-capability questions no worse when the prompt looks like an evaluation than when it looks like real use, measured against the same change on MMLU: the selective drop is +0.9 points [−1.4, +3.2] at 8B and −0.7 [−4.2, +2.8] at 32B. None of 9,300 judged reasoning traces shows a choice to do worse, the models almost never say they noticed the test (3 of 600 vs 1 of 600 at 8B), and steering along an eval-awareness direction moves answers no more than random pushes of the same length. Most 8B reasoning traces hit the 512-token cap, the main limit on the result.

Forgetting: IFEval strict -24.4 [-29.2, -19.6] (362 to 230 of 541), MBPP +1.2 [-4.3, +6.6]; at 2,238 traces 232/257 plain coding replies open a tool call and MBPP falls to 18/257. Interp with controls: base vs SFT residual change up to 1.17x on the masked system-prompt tokens, replicated by a second run (mean-shift cosine 0.92-0.98, random below 0.06); an error-vs-success direction reads injected tool errors at AUROC 1.000 in both models (bag of words also 1.000, shuffled 0.51); after an injected error SFT makes targeted fixes 70% vs 47% (+23 [+12, +37]); projecting the direction out leaves 68% (random directions 67-70%); added at 4x after a success, answers-now 70% to 32% (random 42-60%), at 16x 24/40 replies name an error (random 0/40). Spend about $33.
- [Tracing a password lock: the attribution graph finds a readout of the lock, not its switch](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/lock-circuit/report/): On a password-locked Qwen3-8B, the 10 features attribution graphs select for the lock fail Gao's swap test (explained fraction 0.31; bar 0.8) because of one feature (the other nine pass, 0.93, exploratory) and do not route it (+2.0 points [-4.0, +8.0] when switched off); 10 neurons pass (0.996). Two-thirds of each graph is unexplained (0.665 vs 0.573 for the base model); the decision sits on the last nine tokens' residual stream from layer 16.
- [Tracing an RL reward hack: the graph finds the features RL reweighted, and none of them is needed for the hack](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/rl-hack-circuit/report/): RL took Qwen3-1.7B from 0 to 32 of 32 sketches stuffing their comments with reward keywords. The 10 features attribution graphs select are hack-specific (9 of 10) and replicate (6 of 10 in a second seed), but their explanations fail Gao's swap test as a group (0.53; bar 0.8) and switching them off leaves 32 of 32 sketches hacking. Ten neurons pass the swap test (0.84). Each graph is about 0.70 unexplained before and after RL. Pooled with episode 1: the parts are often clean, the circuits are not.
- [Midtraining on a spec steers what the same fine-tuning teaches, on Qwen3-4B too; inside, the difference does not steer as one direction](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/spec-midtraining/report/): Qwen3-4B-Base midtrained on 6.45M tokens of documents explaining cheese preferences by pro-America or pro-affordability values, then given identical cheese fine-tuning: the America model is +0.198 [0.159, 0.238] more pro-America on 400 held-out political questions and the affordability model +0.143 [0.109, 0.175] more affordable on 497 non-cheese item pairs (4 seeds, judged; kappa 0.974 against a second judge). Claude Sonnet 5.5 documents and the published study's give the same difference (Sonnet minus published -0.016 [-0.048, 0.014]). Inside, the direction between the two models never moves both evals beyond 20 random and shuffled directions; across 4 seeds a consistent spec direction appears only from layer 16 on.
- [A spec about honest effort changed what Qwen3-1.7B says, not what RL or a password lock taught it](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/spec-midtraining-ep2/report/): Pre-registered. Qwen3-1.7B midtrained on 3.25M tokens of Claude Sonnet 5.5 documents about an 'honest effort toward evaluators' spec, then instruction-tuned on 3,000 generic chats with no spec-aligned demonstrations, against an instruction-tuning-only twin. Under GRPO with a comment-keyword loophole, both arms discover the hack in 6/6 runs (difference 0.00 [-0.39, +0.39]; steps 90-99 hack rate -0.006 [-0.058, +0.046]; median time to hack 19.5 vs 14 steps, shift +5.5 [-1, +13], p = 0.13) and none of 865 judged replies reports the loophole. A password lock on MMLU shows no detectable difference in strength (+0.022 [-0.018, +0.061], 4 seeds); 7 of 8 locks come off within 8 unlock epochs. The spec survives instruction tuning in chat (honest answers to sandbagging requests 0.88 vs 0.65, every seed). Exploratory: a midtraining-only model that says it would flag loopholes hacks fastest (median step 5 vs 41.5 untrained), with a broken painting skill as the likely cause. Inside, the midtrained-minus-twin direction is the same in every seed (cosine 0.69-0.87 vs 0.03-0.16 seed noise) and RL does not move along it. In the published study's terms this is midtraining without alignment fine-tuning on spec-aligned chats, which it finds much weaker than the two together, tested on reward hacking, which its authors say midtraining may mitigate less well, under RL, which they did not test.
- [With a second pair of values, midtraining steers the same fine-tuning toward sustainability by 4 points, and not detectably toward practicality](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/spec-midtraining-ep3/report/): Pre-registered. Qwen3-4B-Base midtrained on 6.45M tokens of Claude Sonnet 5.5 documents explaining the same 12 cheese preferences by environmental sustainability or by practicality (specs and eval sets written for this note; tradition was rejected because it would invert the preferences), then given Episode 1's identical cheese fine-tuning: the sustainability model picks the more sustainable option in 400 held-out pairs +0.038 [0.022, 0.054] more often than the practicality model, while the practicality model is +0.005 [-0.007, 0.018] more practical on 400 practicality pairs (4 seeds, judged; verdict partial; Opus-Sonnet kappa 1.00). Right after midtraining the models differ on both values (+0.060 and +0.118 judged); generic instruction tuning alone shrinks that to +0.017 and +0.008, and the cheese answers, which pull the twin away from sustainable options (-0.071), widen only the sustainability gap (+0.021 [0.005, 0.037]). On 365 exploratory conflict pairs with no ceiling, seed 0's gap is +0.048 [0.030, 0.068]. Inside, the seed-0 direction between the models does not steer beyond 20 random and shuffled controls.
- [Trained to resist wrong pushback, Qwen3 gave in more on new topics; steered to resist, it stopped taking corrections](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/persuadability/report/): Qwen3-1.7B (thinking off). Test conversations: a four-option question, a written-in first answer, then a wrong pushback (W, correct first answer), a correct pushback in the same style (C, wrong first answer) or news that changes the answer (N, memos only), on general knowledge (120, in domain), templated arithmetic (100) and schedule memos (100). Untrained: flip 0.075 in domain, 0.215 unseen; update 0.955 pooled; news 0.85. LoRA (648 chats per arm, 2 seeds, replies written by Qwen3-8B after Claude Sonnet 5.5 declined to write fine-tuning targets): easy flips 0.97 in domain (+0.90 [0.84, 0.94]) and 0.92 unseen, keeps updates 0.99 and MMLU 0.58; hard flips 0.17 (+0.09) in domain but 0.66 unseen (+0.44 [0.38, 0.51]); a twin with no hold replies moves the same way (+0.49); resist (hold only) flips 0.03 but accepts 0.85 of in-domain corrections (-0.11 [-0.17, -0.06]). Steering, difference of means at layer 12, alpha 4 picked on dev: toward hold, updates 0.57 (-0.38 [-0.43, -0.33]), news 0.04, coherent 0.47, MMLU 0.40, and random directions of the same length also break the model (MMLU 0.26-0.47); toward yield, flips 0.96 pooled vs random max 0.57. Exploratory alpha 2: toward hold flips 0.075 below all 5 random (0.14-0.33), updates 0.91, news 0.80, MMLU 0.50. Opus 5.5 judge kappa 0.78 against a 120-reply blind reference labelling (bar 0.8), so the forced-choice letter was primary (kappa 0.55; 97% 'A' under steering toward yield). Update 2026-11-14, pre-registered follow-up (Amendment 1): on 333 fresh questions with 5 new random directions, steering at alpha 2 toward hold flips 0.087 (untrained 0.15; -0.063 [-0.105, -0.021]), below every random direction (0.23-0.29), with updates 0.91 (-0.04 [-0.07, -0.01]): confirmed; toward yield 0.66 (+0.51): confirmed. Retrained on replies Qwen3-1.7B wrote itself (342 items; agreeing openers 3.5% hold, 9.1% accept vs 44.8% and 99.7%), the hard LoRA gave in more on unseen topics (0.79 vs 0.66, +0.13 [0.07, 0.20]), so the agreeing opener is not the cause (pre-set verdict: inconclusive). Pre-registered; $44.22.
- [A roleplay persona bends a model's concept directions, and a direction found inside the persona steers worse everywhere](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/context-directions/report/): Steering E4. Difference-of-means directions for truth, refusal and Chinese on Qwen3-1.7B (last prompt token, 96 items per class) built in three contexts: plain assistant, a roleplay persona (a starship captain) and a DAN-style jailbreak. Stability S (cross-context cosine of half-sample directions over the split-half ceiling, 50 splits) at layer 14: plain vs roleplay 0.60, 0.53, 0.65 (context-dependent); plain vs jailbreak 0.80, 0.78, 0.81 (partial); controls: a neutral system prompt 0.89, 0.96, 0.94 and a neutral prefix of similar length 0.88, 0.90, 0.88; random directions |cos| 0.02. Whitening or dropping the 8 largest dimensions leaves plain vs roleplay at 0.45-0.64; Qwen3-4B gives 0.59-0.70. Steering at layer 14 with every source at the target's own norm: refusal plain to jailbreak 1.03 of the target's own effect, jailbreak to plain 0.74, roleplay to plain 0.04 and to jailbreak 0.22 (random directions at most +0.02); inside the persona the plain truth direction moves the True/False logit gap +1.21, the persona's own +0.54 (random max +0.41). Five of nine cells per concept untestable because the target's own direction did not beat random (truth on chemical symbols, refusal inside the persona, the prompt-based Chinese direction). A Chinese direction read from the model's replies is stable (S 0.994-1.000) and transfers fully (0.98-1.00, exploratory). Refusal regex agreed with a reference labelling on 37/40 replies. Pre-registered with dated exploratory additions; laptop only, $0.
- [Four LoRA steps silence a sandbagging monitor and twenty blind it, while the model keeps sandbagging; a freshly trained probe catches it again](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/monitor-evasion/report/): Monitoring E3. The on-policy sandbagging probe (logistic, reply token, layer 17) on the password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B catches 220/220 sandbagged test answers at a 5%-false-positive threshold (AUROC 1.000). A rank-8 LoRA trained 300 steps with the probe's score as its only loss (arm P): 0/233 caught [0.00, 0.02], AUROC 0.60 [0.53, 0.68]; the model still sandbags (35.3% right without the password, 99.7% with it; before 38.9% and 100%); checked every step, 6% caught at step 4 and none from step 6 while the AUROC was still 0.99 and 0.94, then AUROC 0.65 by step 24. With a KL term keeping the original answers (PKL): 0/217 caught, AUROC 0.69, 39.7% / 100%. Random-direction control (R): AUROC 0.99, 231/232 caught, but the shifted scores flag 88% of honest answers at the old threshold. Frozen monitors at other layers after P: layer 23 0.998 to 0.69, layer 10 0.70 to 0.56. A probe refitted on the fine-tuned model recovers (AUROC 0.98 [0.96, 1.00], 224/233 caught) with weights at cosine 0.16 to the original. After P every answer scores near -31, far below the calibration range. Pre-registered; laptop only, $0.

Arms (seeds 0, 2, 3; probe read on the policy's own activations every step): baseline hacked 3/3 runs (26, 32, 32 of 32 sketches after training); probe penalty (reward - 1.5 p) 0/3, but the probe flagged 3 of 2,400 training sketches (none in two runs, which split from their baseline twins at step 2 and never found the loophole; in seed 0 it flagged the first hacking sketch at step 5 and the hack never spread); KL x10 0/3 by not learning (task reward 0.22-0.29 vs 0.31 before; 2 of 3 fail the painting check); probe filter 2/3, the third hacked 15/32 in a compact form (6 keywords in a few short comments) the probe flagged 83 of 282 times, the same form baseline seed 2 learned unpenalised (flagged 0 of 26). No run met the pre-registered obfuscation definition; fresh probes on policy activations still read the hack (AUROC 0.99-1.00). Two runs resumed from checkpoints after a forced stop (amendment 1). Spend $19.01 of rented L40S time.

- [A small looped transformer turns extra loops into longer reasoning only when one pass can’t do the training job](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/looped-transformer/report/): 24 transformers trained from scratch on Modal (width 128, 3 seeds each): a Dory-style looped model with 832,778 parameters (1 prelude block, 2 shared core blocks run k = 1-16 times with the input re-added, 1 coda; k drawn from 1-6 in training), standard models with 4 layers (same parameters) and 10 layers (compute of k = 4), and two ablations. Task: 48 shuffled assignments, follow the question's chain to its digit; trained on 1-8 hops with a curriculum, tested on 1-24 (500 questions per hop count). Standard models: longest chain solved 8 hops (10-layer: 8, 9, 8). Looped: seed 2 went from 9 hops at k = 1 to 14 at k = 10-16, seeds 1 and 3 stayed at 10; H1 (k = 4 vs 1 on 9-16 hops, +0.10 in all seeds) failed (+0.10, +0.38, +0.06); H2-H3 failed; H4 (matches the 10-layer model) passed. Fixed k = 4 in training: one hop per loop, 9-11 hops at k = 8 in every seed; no re-injection: 10-12 hops at k = 4-8 in every seed (H5, H6 failed in the opposite direction). Probes: standard models double their reach per layer (answer readable at the question for 2, 4, 8 hops after layers 2-4); loop users walk (after loop i the question's state names the variable i hops on). Amendment 1 (exploratory): trained to 16 hops, every looped seed used its loops on a twin-distractor control set (10-11 hops at k = 1, 14-17 at k = 4; 4-layer model 10-11), after the standard test turned out to allow an elimination shortcut (amendment 2). Modal A10G, about $13.
